opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest contribution of SWE-bench was changing what people meant by "coding." When we started, most benchmarks for code generation looked like small, self-contained puzzles: here's a function description, write the function. Models were getting very good at those, but that's not what software engineering actually looks like. Real work means being dropped into a large codebase you've never seen, reading an issue that may be vague or incomplete, finding the handful of relevant places across many files, making a change, and not breaking anything else.

So the idea behind SWE-bench was simple: take real GitHub issues from popular open-source Python repositories, along with the pull requests that resolved them, and use the tests from those pull requests to check whether a model's patch actually works. That gave us a measure grounded in real tasks, with an objective way of grading. When we first released it, the results were humbling. The best models could solve only a very small percentage of the problems, in the low single digits. That gap was useful because it showed the community how far we had to go, and it gave people a clear target.

SWE-agent was the natural next step. We saw that you can't expect a model to solve these problems in one shot from a static prompt. A developer explores, runs the code, looks at errors, and iterates, so the model needed to be able to do that too. One of the key lessons was how much the interface between the model and the computer matters. We talked about this as agent-computer interface design, analogous to human-computer interaction. Small choices, such as how you show a file, how search results are summarized, or whether a linter catches a bad edit right away, made a big difference in performance, even with the same underlying model.

What's been gratifying is seeing how far things moved once there was a shared benchmark and an open harness to build on. Labs and startups started reporting on it, and scores climbed dramatically in a fairly short time. The benchmark also has limitations, of course. As systems improve, you have to worry about overfitting and test quality, and the benchmark doesn't capture everything, like long-term maintainability, or working with people to clarify what they want. That means we need to keep evolving the evaluations toward harder, more realistic tasks. But I think the lasting contribution is that framing: evaluate these systems on real work, in real environments, and treat the agent's whole loop as the thing you're building, not just the model.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that SWE-bench did two things at once, and it's worth separating them.

The first was just raising the bar on what "evaluating a coding model" meant. Before that, most of the benchmarks were function-level: here's a docstring, write the body, we'll run a few unit tests. That's a real skill, but it's not what software engineers spend their days doing. We wanted tasks where you're dropped into a real repository with a real issue someone actually filed, and you have to figure out where the problem lives, make a change that fits the existing codebase, and not break anything else. Pulling those from actual GitHub pull requests, with the repository's own tests as the judge, meant the task distribution was grounded in reality rather than in what we imagined was hard. And the initial numbers were humbling. The best systems were solving a couple percent of instances. That was useful information, because it told everyone how far the gap was between "good at coding puzzles" and "useful on a real engineering task."

The second contribution, and I'd argue the more lasting one, was SWE-agent, because it reframed the problem. The insight was that the model isn't the whole system. A language model dropped into a raw bash shell does badly, not because it can't reason about code, but because the interface is hostile. It gets flooded with output, it can't see where it is in a file, it edits things and silently introduces syntax errors. So we built what we called an agent-computer interface: a small, deliberate set of tools for searching, viewing files in windows, editing with linting feedback. Just designing that interface well roughly quadrupled performance with the same underlying model. That was a bit of a wake-up call for me personally. It said that a lot of the leverage in making these systems useful lives in the scaffolding and the feedback loops, not only in the weights.

Where I think it's had the most impact on progress is that it gave the field a shared target that was hard enough to drive real work. You saw labs and open-source groups build better agents, better retrieval, better verification strategies, and you could actually compare them. Scores went from low single digits to the point where the verified subset is largely saturated, which happened faster than I expected.

I'd also be candid about the limits. Any benchmark built from public repositories is going to leak into training data over time, and we have to be clear-eyed about that. The tasks skew toward Python and toward issues that had clean test coverage, which is not the whole world of software. And passing the tests isn't the same as writing code a reviewer would merge. So I see SWE-bench less as the finish line and more as proof that evaluating on realistic, executable tasks is feasible. The next versions, and the things other groups have built on top of it, are pushing toward more languages, longer-horizon tasks, and judging quality rather than just correctness. That's the direction I'm excited about.

r002.rationale: The response discusses realistic benchmark tasks drawn from GitHub issues and pull requests, but does not identify training data covering software-engineering workflows beyond code as a missing ingredient.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts function-level benchmarks with tasks in real repositories that require resolving actual issues, changing code, and avoiding regressions.

astra-6.text:
I think they address two complementary problems. SWE-bench gives us a way to measure progress on software engineering tasks that look much more like real work. You have an existing repository and an issue to resolve, so you need to understand the code, locate the relevant pieces, make a change, and check that it works. That’s a richer problem than generating a standalone function from a description.

SWE-agent addresses how you enable a language model to do that work. What tools does it have to navigate the repository, edit files, and run tests? How do you present the results of those actions so it can decide what to do next? The interface matters quite a bit: having a capable model is only part of the solution.

Together, they give us a useful feedback loop. The benchmark exposes where systems struggle, and the agent harness lets us explore how better interactions with the environment can help. I wouldn’t equate solving benchmark issues with handling every aspect of software engineering, but it’s a concrete step toward systems that can work within real codebases.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they make two complementary contributions. SWE-bench gives us a way to measure progress on real software engineering problems: you have an issue from a repository, and the system has to make a change that resolves it. That requires more than generating a function from a description. You have to find the relevant code, understand how different pieces interact, and test your hypothesis.

SWE-agent explores how to give a language model the tools to do that work. How does it navigate a repository, inspect files, edit code, and get feedback from running tests? The interface matters a lot. Even with the same underlying model, changing how it interacts with the environment can make a substantial difference.

Together, they help us study both the capabilities of the model and the system around it. I wouldn’t equate solving benchmark issues with doing the full job of a software engineer, but it’s a useful step toward evaluating agents on concrete, realistic tasks.
